Out back

Eight thousand square feet of beer garden.

Picnic tables on the lawn, a fire pit, a covered deck for when it rains, and a stage for when there’s music.

Inside is a museum you can drink in — an elk over the booths, a pressed-tin ceiling, the Rainier “R” glowing in the window, a pool table, and walls covered in the town’s mining-and-logging days. Outside is where the afternoon goes.

What’s around

The Carbon River, hiking, biking and horseback trails, the ORV park, the Wilkeson coke ovens and the mining ghost towns up the canyon.

True story

The general came home for lunch.

Three people sat down for burgers and asked Amber if anyone famous ever came out of Carbonado. She named two — then mentioned the kid from town who grew up to be the most decorated living soldier. He was the one asking. Maj. Gen. Patrick Brady, Medal of Honor, “Dustoff 55,” was showing his friends where he grew up.

His challenge coin sits on the bar. Her copy of Dead Men Flying is signed.

The story

The canteen that wouldn’t quit.

Before it was a bar it was the post office, a barber’s corner and a dentist’s office — and for most of its life it’s been the place this town drinks.

When the Carbon Hill Coal Company ran Carbonado it owned the whole shebang — the houses, the brick store across the street, and this place. Miners were paid in scrip; rent came out first and whatever was left went to the Company Store or the Canteen. Even so, moonshine ran out of the woods, and at the peak the town kept three taverns busy. Draft beer came late; hard liquor didn’t reach the back bar until the ’90s.

Canteen, then Tavern, now Saloon. A town that once ran one of the biggest mines on the Pacific Coast is now one of the smallest incorporated towns in Washington — and this is still the only bar in it.

  1. 1878

    Built

    Goes up in the coal camp, across from the Company’s brick store.

  2. 1889

    Moved & opened

    Hauled to Pershing Avenue and opened as the Company’s “Canteen” — the first bar in town.

  3. 1937

    Company quits

    Homes sold off; the Canteen carries on in private hands — Coke cooler and candy counter for the kids.

  4. 2012

    Marked historic

    E Clampus Vitus raises the historical marker out front.

  5. 2026

    Still here

    Same building, same corner.

Find us

End of the road. On purpose.

Heads up, driversThe Fairfax Bridge south of town on SR-165 closed for good in April 2025, so there’s no through-road to Mowich Lake anymore. Carbonado is the destination now — come up, eat, and head back the way you came.

  1. From Enumclaw

    SR-410 west to Buckley, then SR-165 south through Wilkeson. About 20 minutes.

  2. Into Carbonado

    Follow 165 into town and find Pershing Avenue. The red building with the flag on the porch is us.
